Question 6
\[
f(x)= \begin{cases}\frac{\cos x-1}{x^{2}} & \text { for } x \neq 0 \\ -\frac{1}{2} & \text { for } x=0\end{cases}
\]
The function \(f\), defined above, has derivatives of all orders. Let \(g\) be the function defined by \(g(x)=1+\int_{0}^{x} f(t) d t\).
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Write the first three nonzero terms and the general term of the Taylor series for \(\cos x\) about \(x=0\). Use this series to write the first three nonzero terms and the general term of the Taylor series for \(f\) about \(x=0\).
\item[(b)] Use the Taylor series for \(f\) about \(x=0\) found in part (a) to determine whether \(f\) has a relative maximum, relative minimum, or neither at \(x=0\). Give a reason for your answer.
\item[(c)] Write the fifth-degree Taylor polynomial for \(g\) about \(x=0\).
\item[(d)] The Taylor series for \(g\) about \(x=0\), evaluated at \(x=1\), is an alternating series with individual terms that decrease in absolute value to 0. Use the third-degree Taylor polynomial for \(g\) about \(x=0\) to estimate the value of \(g(1)\). Explain why this estimate differs from the actual value of \(g(1)\) by less than \(\frac{1}{6!}\).
\item[(a)] \(\quad \cos (x)=1-\frac{x^{2}}{2}+\frac{x^{4}}{4!}-\cdots+(-1)^{n} \frac{x^{2 n}}{(2 n)!}+\cdots\)
\[
f(x)=-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{x^{2}}{4!}-\frac{x^{4}}{6!}+\cdots+(-1)^{n+1} \frac{x^{2 n}}{(2 n+2)!}+\cdots
\]
\item[(b)] \(f^{\prime}(0)\) is the coefficient of \(x\) in the Taylor series for \(f\) about \(x=0\), so \(f^{\prime}(0)=0\).
\[
\begin{aligned}
& \frac{f^{\prime \prime}(0)}{2!}=\frac{1}{4!} \text { is the coefficient of } x^{2} \text { in the Taylor series for } f \text { about } \\
& x=0, \text { so } f^{\prime \prime}(0)=\frac{1}{12} .
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, by the Second Derivative Test, \(f\) has a relative minimum at \(x=0\).
\item[(c)] \(P_{5}(x)=1-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{x^{3}}{3 \cdot 4!}-\frac{x^{5}}{5 \cdot 6!}\)
\item[(d)] \(g(1) \approx 1-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{3 \cdot 4!}=\frac{37}{72}\)
\end{itemize}
Since the Taylor series for \(g\) about \(x=0\) evaluated at \(x=1\) is
\begin{itemize}
\item[] \(3:\left\{\begin{aligned} 1 & : \text { terms for } \cos x \\ 2 & : \text { terms for } f \\ 1 & : \text { first three terms } \\ 1 & : \text { general term }\end{aligned}\right.\)
\item[] \(2:\left\{\begin{array}{l}1: \text { determines } f^{\prime}(0) \\ 1: \text { answer with reason }\end{array}\right.\)
\item[] \(2:\left\{\begin{array}{l}1: \text { two correct terms } \\ 1: \text { remaining terms }\end{array}\right.\)
\item[] \(2:\left\{\begin{array}{l}1 \text { : estimate } \\ 1 \text { : explanation }\end{array}\right.\)
\end{itemize} alternating and the terms decrease in absolute value to 0, we know
\[
\left|g(1)-\frac{37}{72}\right|<\frac{1}{5 \cdot 6!}<\frac{1}{6!} .
\]
